items.stem: For every integer n, which statement must be true?

options.text: n² − n is a multiple of 3

items.worked_solution: n² − n = n(n − 1). Two consecutive integers have opposite parity, so their product is even. Counterexample n = 2 disproves divisibility by 4 and by 3; n = 0 disproves positivity.
items.misconception: Distinguish always-true claims from statements that work for only some integers.

items.stem: How many real values of x satisfy |x − 2| + |x + 1| = 5?
items.worked_solution: For −1 ≤ x ≤ 2, the sum equals 3, so no solutions. For x < −1, the sum is 1 − 2x = 5, giving x = −2. For x > 2, the sum is 2x − 1 = 5, giving x = 3. Both satisfy their intervals, so exactly two real solutions.
items.misconception: Split absolute-value equations at both sign-change points, then check candidate domains.

items.stem: A real number t satisfies t² − 4t + 7 = k. Which of the following is the complete set of possible values of k?
items.worked_solution: Complete the square: t² − 4t + 7 = (t − 2)² + 3. Since a real square is nonnegative, k ≥ 3. Equality occurs at t = 2, and every larger value is attained by t = 2 + √(k − 3).
items.misconception: An attainable minimum must be included in the range.
